topic: Thread Blocking: Implicit Synchronization in `std::future` Destructors
explanation: Assumption: All `std::future` objects are lightweight handles that can be safely destroyed at any time. Reality: If a `std::future` refers to a shared state generated by a non-deferred task launched via `std::async`, its destructor implicitly calls `wait()`. Why It Fails: This forces the thread executing the destructor (e.g., when a container holding futures is destroyed, or a class member future goes out of scope) to block until the associated asynchronous task completes. This mechanism, designed to prevent the C++ runtime from terminating a running task, introduces non-obvious synchronization points and potential performance bottlenecks.
practical_example: A class destructor designed to be fast accidentally holds a member `std::future` tied to a long-running computation initiated by `std::async`. When an object of this class is destroyed, the entire application thread unexpectedly stalls, waiting for the background computation to finish.
chapter: Item 38: Differentiate between thread-based and task-based programming
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
